newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Currency board will boost confidence - Bulgaria PM.
newsitem.headline: Currency board will boost confidence - Bulgaria PM.

text.p: Bulgaria's reformist Prime Minister Ivan Kostov said the IMF-prescribed currency board system introduced on Tuesday will stabilise the crisis-ridden economy and enable the government to borrow on global markets.

In an interview with Reuters and Reuters Financial Television broadcast on Tuesday, Kostov said the government was considering issuing Eurobonds as a signal of economic stabilisation once it has launched the restrictive system to regulate the country's money supply.

"By implementing financial discipline and by stabilising the Bulgarian monetary and banking system, (the currency board) will allow a long term interest rate reduction that will promote investment in Bulgaria and will enable us to bottom out," said Kostov.
Borrowing on external markets to service a three trillion lev ($1.8 billion) domestic debt and fund a restrictive budget is an option being considered by the government, which took office in May.
The currency board system bans central bank lending to the government and commercial banks and requires that levs in circulation be fully covered by foreign exchange reserves.
Under Bulgaria's currency board arangement, the central bank guarantees that it will have one mark for every thousand levs in circulation, freezing the exchange rate at that level.
The government hopes to fund part of a 6.2 percent of GDP budget deficit with $320 million revenue from sell-offs.

"In principle we are discussing the idea of placing Eurobonds, more as a signal that things in Bulgaria have changed and that risk has decreased and Bulgaria is a country worthy of investors' confidence," said Kostov.
Before entering global markets, Bulgaria is likely to seek a new credit rating towards the end of the year that will reflect a possible economic improvement.

Kostov saw the closure of loss-making state firms and the ensuing increase of unemployment rate as a major short-term challenge for the government. Bulgaria stands to receive an $80 million World Bank loan to set up a safety net for the jobless and the poor.

Another risk in the currency board operation would be sustaining the fixed exchange rate over several years, which may become difficult if at some moment inflation gets out of control and undermines the competitive power of local producers.

"The major problem is that if we do not succeed in curbing inflation it will reduce the competitive power of Bulgarian producers. If we fail to control this, the current peg rate will come under pressure and in several years we will have to revalue it," said Kostov.
"But I believe that the Bulgarian economy will have the strength to boost efficiency and to raise production output."
The government's stringent monetary policy, backed by a $510 million standby agreement with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) since March, has led to a noticeable stabilisation.

Inflation has since then steadily declined to 5.6 percent in May and minus 0.7 percent in April from 243 percent in February. Interest rates have come down to 1.27 percent monthly from 18 percent in March.
The lev has traded steady at around 1,600 to the dollar and 950 to the mark in the past three months, after nosediving to 3,000 per dollar in February pressed by political and economic turmoil.
"I think that pegging the lev to the German mark will help Bulgaria adjust more easily to the European Monetary Union," Kostov said.

Pegging the lev to the mark will synchronise Bulgaria's economic cycles with those of the EU in the long term, while the restrictions of the currency board system will bring Bulgaria closer to EU admission criteria, economists say. -- Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-981-4145
